posts.title: Building in public without the noise
posts.excerpt: A practical way to share what you learn, protect your focus, and turn small experiments into useful writing.
body: Writing online does not require a grand announcement or a perfect personal brand. Start with a small, specific lesson that could help someone solve a real problem.
Keep a note on your phone. When you fix a bug, make a decision, test an idea, or learn something surprising, capture the context and the lesson in a few sentences.
Before publishing, remove private information, customer details, access tokens, internal screenshots, and anything you do not have permission to share.
Consistency is more useful than urgency. A clear article published regularly is better than a rushed post written only to keep up with a trend.

posts.title: Small notes lead to better decisions
posts.excerpt: A simple note-taking habit can help you spot patterns and explain why you made a choice.
body: When a decision is fresh, write down the problem, the options you considered, and why you chose one.
A month later, that short note can save time. You can see whether the assumptions were correct and what you would change next time.
Keep the habit small enough to maintain. Three useful sentences are a good start.

posts.title: A calmer approach to learning
posts.excerpt: Build a sustainable learning loop instead of trying to master everything at once.
body: Choose one skill that matters for your current work. Define a tiny outcome you can complete in one session.
After the session, write what worked, what confused you, and what you will try next. This turns passive consumption into active practice.
Review the notes weekly. Progress often becomes visible only after you look back.

posts.title: A practical guide to web performance
posts.excerpt: A checklist for finding the bottlenecks that make a website feel slow.
body: Start with field data where available, then use browser performance tools to identify the largest sources of delay.

list: Avoid unnecessary JavaScript on the initial route.
Cache static assets with appropriate headers.
Measure Core Web Vitals and test on slower devices.

body: Optimisation is an iterative process. Change one thing, measure again, and keep the improvements that help real users.

posts.title: How to write useful technical notes
posts.excerpt: Turn debugging sessions and hard-won lessons into documentation you will actually reuse.
body: A good technical note records the context, the symptom, the reason, and the fix—not just the final command.
Add a small example and a date if the information may become stale. Keep credentials and sensitive logs out of the note.
Review notes periodically and turn recurring lessons into reusable documentation.

posts.title: Designing a small product around real work
posts.excerpt: Start with a narrow problem, a clear user, and the smallest workflow that saves them time.
body: A small product can be valuable when it solves a repeated problem clearly and reliably.
Talk to potential users about their current workflow. Look for repeated friction rather than beginning with a long feature list.
Build the smallest useful version, observe where people struggle, and improve from evidence.
